Why Are We Doing This?

For the past couple of weeks, I’ve been tricking you. We’ve been measuring cooling drinks and plotting exponential decay, but what we were actually doing was solving your very first differential equation. Today, we are going to put a formal name to that math, see how it applies to everything from your bank account to cockroach populations, and then level it up. We are going to transition from tracking how things change in just time to tracking how they change in both time and space—which brings us to the messy, fascinating, and often misunderstood world of diffusion.

TL;DR — Key Takeaways

We formalized the math behind exponential growth and decay using a first-order linear homogeneous differential equation, where the rate of change of a function is proportional to the function itself. We then introduced the diffusion equation (Fick’s Second Law), which uses partial derivatives to track how concentration changes over both time and position. Through a live drink demonstration and some literature review, we discovered that most macroscopic “diffusion” demos (like dropping food coloring in a beaker) are actually showing drift driven by gravity and temperature gradients. True diffusion is a random walk that is incredibly slow on the macro scale, which is exactly why biological cells have to be so microscopically small.

Learning Objectives

By the end of these notes, you should be able to:

  • Identify the components of a first-order linear homogeneous differential equation.

  • Verify that an exponential function is a valid solution to this type of ODE.

  • Explain the physical difference between a standard derivative and a partial derivative.

  • Distinguish between drift (directed motion) and diffusion (random walk) in physical systems.

  • Set up a 1D random walk simulation using dice and paper.

Before You Start

You should be comfortable with basic calculus, specifically taking the derivative of an exponential function (e.g., knowing that the derivative of e^{ax} is a e^{ax}). You should also recall our recent experiments tracking the temperature deviation of cooling drinks, as that physical system is the foundation for the math we are formalizing today.

The “Fancy” Equation We’ve Already Been Solving

Let’s do a little bird’s-eye overview of the math we’ve been doing over the past couple of weeks. We’ve been looking at exponential decay, and in doing so, you’ve been working with something that has a very fancy name: a first-order linear homogeneous differential equation.

Despite the intimidating name, the concept is straightforward. On one side of the equation, you have the time derivative of something—how much that something is changing as a function of time. On the other side, you have a constant (which we’ll call r for the rate) multiplying that exact same something.

In plain English: How much something is changing is equal to the rate multiplied by the amount of the something.

Mathematically, we write this as: \begin{equation} \tag{1} \frac{df}{dt} = r \cdot f(t) \end{equation} where:

  • f(t) is the “something” (a function that depends on time t).

  • \frac{df}{dt} is the time derivative (how fast f(t) is changing).

  • r is the decay rate or growth rate (a constant).

What is the “Something”?

What is this f(t) in the real world? It should be painfully clear based on our recent labs: it’s temperature! More specifically, it is the temperature deviation, \Delta T = T - T_a (where T_a is the ambient room temperature). Because the drink is cooling down, the rate r is negative (r < 0).

But we didn’t actually do an experiment on other systems. What else could be growing or decaying exponentially?

  • Money: My investment account (that’s wishful thinking, but it models exponential growth where r > 0).

  • Biology: Population growth of something undesirable, like cockroaches or pathogens (r > 0).

  • Technology: Moore’s Law, tracking the number of transistors per chip area over time (r > 0).

Notice that the “something” is not just a single number; it is a function that has a shape you can graph. If r < 0, the function decays toward zero. If r > 0, the function blows up to a really large number as time goes on.

Key Takeaway

The shape of the solution function is always the same—it’s an exponential curve, f(t) \propto e^{rt}. The only difference between explosive growth and gradual decay is the sign of the constant r.

Checking Our Work

Strictly speaking, solving a differential equation means finding the function that makes the equation true. If you are comfortable with integration, you can solve Equation (1) directly. But in this class, my goal is to show you standard differential equations you’ll see over and over in STEM, show you what the solution looks like, and prove that it works.

If a random stranger tells you, “Hey, the solution to this differential equation is f(t) = e^{rt},” you don’t have to take their word for it. You can check it!

How do we verify that f(t) = e^{rt} is the correct solution?

We plug it back into the original differential equation. We take the time derivative of e^{rt} and see if it equals r \cdot e^{rt}.

Let’s do that easy-peasy one-step check. We want to evaluate \frac{d}{dt}(e^{rt}). Here, t is our variable, and r is a constant that doesn’t depend on time. The rule for differentiating an exponential is that you pull the constant out in front and keep the rest the same: \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}(e^{rt}) = r \cdot e^{rt} \tag{2} \end{equation} Look at that! The left side equals the right side. The derivative of exponential growth is still exponential growth. The math checks out.

Leveling Up: The Diffusion Equation

Now I want us to move on to a second differential equation. It sounds less intimidating than the first one, but it is mathematically more complicated. It is called the Diffusion Equation, also known as the Heat Equation, or Fick’s Second Law.

Here is what it looks like: \begin{equation} \tag{3} \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2} \end{equation}

Let’s break down these new symbols. First, you’ll notice we aren’t using the normal d for our derivatives. We are using the lowercase Greek letter delta (\partial). This symbol means we are taking a partial derivative.

Why do we need a partial derivative? In our cooling drink example, temperature deviation was a function of time only. We just stuck a thermometer in one spot and watched the clock. We didn’t care about position.

But with diffusion—like heat spreading through a house, or electrons diffusing across a semiconductor—the concentration C depends on both time (t) and position (x). We write this as C(x,t).

Key Takeaway

When a function depends on more than one variable (like position and time), and you want to take the derivative with respect to just one of them, you use a partial derivative (\partial).

So, the left side of Equation (3), \frac{\partial C}{\partial t}, is the time derivative: how the concentration changes as the clock ticks.

The right side features D, which is the diffusivity (or diffusion coefficient). This is a constant specific to your physical system and material. It multiplies \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2}, which is the second partial derivative of concentration with respect to position. (If you take the derivative of a derivative, you get the second derivative, just like in normal calculus).

The Kool-Aid Lie: Drift vs. Diffusion

To see this in action, I brought in some water, Sprite, food coloring, and an open bag of purple Kool-Aid. In class, I had everyone pour a drink and drop a pinch of Kool-Aid or a drop of food coloring into their cup.

When you drop food coloring into a cup of water, it immediately starts swirling around and coloring the liquid. Is this diffusion?

No! It looks like it, but it is actually a process called drift (or convection).

When you drop the dye in, it turns red instantly and you see stuff swirling around as it spreads. But that is not diffusion. Diffusion happens via a random walk (which we will simulate shortly). What you are seeing in the cup is drift.

Drift is directed motion driven by a force or a field. What forces are acting on the dye in your cup?

  • Gravity: The food coloring and Kool-Aid are slightly denser/heavier than water, so they sink.

  • Thermal Gradients: Some parts of the liquid are warmer than others, causing convection currents.

  • Fluid Movement: Air flow over the open cup, or the residual swirling from when you poured the drink, physically pushes the dye around.

In semiconductors, we see drift when electrons are driven by an external battery or an electric field. They drift along or against the field.

I actually looked into this before class. Someone went the extra mile to set up a strictly diffusive experiment. To stop drift, they had to use a thin test tube, seal it to stop air currents, keep the temperature uniform, and use salt water so the dye would float rather than sink.

When all that drift was eliminated, they found that true diffusion is orders of magnitude slower than what we saw in the cup. It took hours for the dye to travel just 1 centimeter! The mathematical relationship for diffusion distance (x_D) over time (t) is actually x_D \propto \sqrt{D \cdot t}.

This explains a massive biological mystery: why are cells so small? Why don’t we have elephant-sized single cells? Because cells rely on diffusion to get oxygen and nutrients. If a cell were 1 millimeter wide, it would take 40 minutes for oxygen to diffuse across it. But over a distance of 10 microns (the size of a typical cell), diffusion takes less than a second. Diffusion is terrible at macro-scales, but incredibly efficient at micro-scales.

Side note: If you mixed Kool-Aid into Sprite during the demo, you can drink it. If you don’t like it, dump it in the sink on your way out. I just don’t want anybody to say that you were poisoned in this class.

Simulating a Random Walk

Since true diffusion is a random walk, we are going to simulate it. We didn’t have time to finish this in class, but we got the environment set up so we can hit the ground running next time.

We are playing a game of diffusion—kind of like Yahtzee.

The Setup: Take a sheet of paper and fold it in half repeatedly (taco or burger style) until you have 16 distinct vertical sections or “slots.” Draw lines down the folds to make it clear. This represents our 1-dimensional spatial environment (the x-axis).

Next, make 16 “particles” out of scrap paper and number them 1 through 16. To start, we place all 16 particles in the middle of our environment (8 in the middle-left slot, 8 in the middle-right slot). This represents a high initial concentration C(x,t=0) at the center.

The Rules: For each particle, you roll a standard six-sided die.

  • If you roll an odd number, the particle moves one slot to the right.

  • If you roll an even number, the particle moves one slot to the left.

You go through all 16 particles, moving them based on the dice roll. Once all 16 have moved, that represents one “time step” (t=1). You take a picture with your smartphone to record the concentration profile.

Then, you do it again for Step 2, Step 3, and so forth. Over time, purely through random chance, the particles will spread out from the center. This is the fundamental mechanism of diffusion!

Key Terms
First-Order Linear Homogeneous ODE

A differential equation where the rate of change of a function is directly proportional to the function itself (e.g., \frac{df}{dt} = r \cdot f).

Partial Derivative (\partial)

A derivative taken with respect to one variable while holding other variables constant. Used when a function depends on multiple things, like position and time.

Diffusivity (D)

A constant that describes how easily a specific substance spreads through a specific medium.

Drift

Directed motion of particles driven by an external force or field (like gravity, temperature gradients, or electric fields).

Random Walk

A mathematical process where an object takes successive steps in random directions. This is the microscopic mechanism that drives macroscopic diffusion.

What to Review: Brush up on your basic derivative rules, specifically how to take the derivative of an exponential function (e^{rt}). Also, make sure you understand the difference between a standard derivative (d) and a partial derivative (\partial).

What’s Next: Bring your folded paper and 16 particles to our next class! We will hit the ground running, rolling the dice to simulate our random walk, and we’ll see how this simple game of chance perfectly maps onto the fancy partial differential equation we learned today.
